analysis.one_liner: Rebuilds the wall between everyday bank deposits and Wall Street trading and insurance businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it died in committee with 8 cosponsors before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would restore a modern version of the Glass-Steagall rules that separated ordinary banking from Wall Street until they were repealed in 1999. Insured banks could no longer own or affiliate with securities firms, insurance companies, or swap dealers; banks could not trade for their own profit, underwrite securities, or invest in hedge funds and private equity. Banks would be limited to core services like taking deposits, making loans, and running payment systems, and executives would have to sign sworn statements that their firms comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers gain the most: money protected by federal deposit insurance could no longer sit inside the same company as high-risk trading, derivatives, and insurance operations, reducing the chance that taxpayers are pulled into a bailout. Bank customers would face fewer conflicts of interest, since banks could no longer profit by pushing products in which they hold their own positions.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository banks from being affiliated with, or under common ownership with, any insurance company, securities entity, or swaps entity.

Limits national banks to core banking services — receiving deposits, extending credit, payment systems, and limited securities investment — and bars them from underwriting securities or trading for their own account.
Prohibits bank holding companies from proprietary trading, market-making, prime brokerage, and owning, sponsoring, or investing in hedge funds or private equity funds.
Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that had allowed financial holding companies to combine commercial banking, investment banking, and insurance since 1999.

Adds an anti-evasion rule with a penalty of 10 percent of a firm's three-year average net profits, and requires bank executives to attest in writing, under penalty of perjury, that their firm is not engaged in prohibited activities.

The bill's own findings cite the JPMorgan 'Whale Trades' episode, in which traders made risky derivatives bets using deposits partly insured by the federal government, as the kind of behavior the separation would prevent.

analysis.who_pays: Large Wall Street banking companies would bear the cost: they would have up to five years to divest trading, insurance, and derivatives businesses that generate substantial profits, and their ability to fund trading with insured deposits and an implicit 'too big to fail' guarantee would end. Some customers could lose the convenience of getting securities and insurance products through their bank.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals bankruptcy-code provisions (sections 555, 559, 560, and 562) that let derivatives and repo counterparties immediately terminate and settle contracts when a firm fails; critics of removing these 'safe harbors' argue that doing so can make a bankruptcy messier and spread losses to other firms.

The bill would not restrict risky trading at standalone investment banks and funds that simply stay outside the banking system — it only bars them from affiliating with insured banks — so some of the risk it targets could migrate rather than disappear.

Existing affiliations would have to be terminated within five years (with limited extensions), a forced restructuring that would carry real transition costs and could strip customers of one-stop banking, securities, and insurance services they currently use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — separating government-insured deposits from speculative trading and reducing the taxpayer backstop for 'too big to fail' firms — is real and directly answers a problem documented in the bill's own findings, including the JPMorgan whale-trades episode. The costs are borne almost entirely by large financial firms, though the five-year forced divestiture would be disruptive and the bill would leave risk-taking in the unaffiliated securities industry untouched. On balance, the bill is a serious structural fix rather than a poorly designed one, but it never got far enough for its design to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2015, sent to the House Financial Services and Judiciary Committees, referred to a Financial Services subcommittee two weeks later, and then sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Capuano introduced the bill on July 14, 2015, joined as original cosponsors by Rep. Walter Jones (R-NC), Rep. Katherine Clark (D-MA), and Rep. Ted Yoho (R-FL).

The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and, for relevant provisions, the House Judiciary Committee, and on July 29, 2015 it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No further action was ever taken on the bill, and it never received a committee markup, floor vote, or companion movement in the Senate before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Wall Street banking companies came out ahead: they kept the ability to combine federally insured deposits with proprietary trading, derivatives, hedge fund, and insurance businesses, and no new separation rules were added. No member ever had to cast a recorded vote on the question.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large Wall Street banks kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill had genuine bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat introduced it with two Republican original cosponsors, and the full cosponsor list was 6 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of any opposition does not appear in the record.

industries.industry: Large universal banks (bank holding companies combining commercial banking with trading)
industries.note: These firms would have to divest trading, underwriting, market-making, and prime brokerage businesses within five years, ending their ability to fund trading with insured deposits and an implicit too-big-to-fail guarantee. Their gain under the status quo is the public's exposure to bailouts, so their interest in blocking the bill ran against ordinary depositors and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Securities and investment banking firms affiliated with bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that let financial holding companies own securities businesses, forcing a separation. Standalone securities firms outside the banking system would be unaffected, but they could no longer be acquired by or merged with insured banks.

Insured banks could no longer affiliate with, be commonly owned with, or act as insurance companies, unwinding bank-insurance combinations permitted since 1999. Customers would have to buy insurance products outside their bank.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity firms
industries.note: Bank holding companies could no longer own, sponsor, or invest in hedge funds or private equity funds, cutting off a funding and distribution channel supplied by big banks.

Banks and holding companies could not deal or make markets in exchange-traded or over-the-counter swaps, shrinking the dealer market, though the bill explicitly preserves banks' ability to buy swaps as end users to hedge their own interest-rate and currency exposures.

Smaller banks engaged mainly in core banking would face little disruption while large diversified competitors were forced to slim down, and the taxpayer guarantee would be pointed back toward plain vanilla banking. The bill's findings note the crisis-era trend toward consolidation among a few large institutions.
